subsection: 1. Concepts of work and attitudes to work

notes.b: Work is any activity that produces goods or services. It falls into three types, which differ in whether they are paid and who benefits.
points: Paid employment: work done for a wage or salary, usually under a contract of employment between employer and employee.
Self-employment is also paid work: the worker earns income directly from their own trade, business or profession and carries its financial risk.
Unpaid work: done without financial reward, mainly in the home, such as housework, cooking, cleaning, child care and care of elderly or disabled relatives.
Home-related activities such as DIY, home maintenance, gardening and household budgeting are also unpaid work.
Voluntary work: unpaid work done by choice for people outside the household, usually through a charity, community group or organisation.
Paid employment carries entitlement to PRSI-based social insurance and, in many jobs, pension, sick pay and paid holidays.

notes.h: Job descriptions as a starting point
notes.b: A job description sets out what a post involves. It is the basis for judging how satisfying the work is likely to be.
points: A job description usually states the job title, main duties and responsibilities, working hours, place of work, pay range and the qualifications or skills needed.
Duties involving planning, decision-making or creativity suggest scope for intrinsic satisfaction.
Routine, repetitive duties with a fixed pay scale suggest that satisfaction depends mainly on extrinsic rewards.
Flexible hours, job-sharing or home working in a description indicate conditions that can improve work-life balance.
Method: list the duties, match each one to the intrinsic or extrinsic satisfaction it offers, then identify one change that would raise satisfaction.

notes.b: Extrinsic satisfaction comes from rewards linked to work rather than from the task itself.
points: Sources: pay, bonuses, pension, paid holidays, job security, and company benefits such as a car or private health insurance.
Repetitive, uninteresting work, such as assembly-line production, may leave pay as the main source of satisfaction.
Satisfaction is also gained by spending income on goods, leisure and socialising outside work.
Extrinsic rewards can sustain a worker in a job, but on their own they bring less pride and self-esteem.

notes.b: Intrinsic satisfaction comes from the work itself: the fulfilment, pleasure and creativity it offers.
points: Sources: challenge and variety in tasks; autonomy and responsibility; the chance to use skills; pride in a finished task.
Work builds self-esteem, confidence and independence.
Work can confer status and respect in the community, meeting social and psychological needs.
Intrinsic satisfaction is strongest when a job matches a person's skills and interests.

notes.b: Work ethic is the attitude a person brings to work. Work attainment is the level of achievement and advancement reached through work.
points: Work ethic is shown through punctuality, low absenteeism, commitment to tasks, and respect for authority and colleagues.
Employers value a strong work ethic, and it is linked to promotion and good references.
Work attainment reflects results such as promotion, added responsibility, qualifications gained and recognition from colleagues.
A positive attitude and strong work ethic make a worker more likely to be promoted and trusted with responsibility.

notes.h: Factors that shape attitudes to work
points: Working conditions: part-time work, job-sharing, flexitime and working from home make work-life balance easier.
Atmosphere at work, including relationships with supervisors and colleagues, affects how workers feel about their jobs.
Personal identity: some occupations confer status in the community, which can encourage a positive attitude to work.
Social contact: a workplace meets social needs, and peer pressure influences how seriously a worker takes the job.
Background and experience: family attitudes to work, education and earlier work experience shape expectations.

notes.h: Variation in attitudes according to occupation
points: Occupations differ in the mix of intrinsic and extrinsic satisfaction they offer.
Professional and creative occupations often give high intrinsic satisfaction through responsibility, autonomy and recognised expertise.
Repetitive manual and production jobs tend to depend more on pay, job security and working conditions.
Shift work and unsocial hours can reduce satisfaction in occupations such as nursing and emergency services unless flexibility is offered.
Self-employed workers often report high intrinsic satisfaction because they control their own hours and methods, but they bear greater financial risk.

notes.b: Satisfaction can be judged by checking both sources of satisfaction and the factors that undermine them.
points: Questions to ask: is the worker paid fairly, is the employment secure, and is effort recognised?
Variety in tasks, training and clear routes to promotion increase intrinsic satisfaction.
Taking part in decisions, teamwork and a safe, pleasant workplace raise satisfaction.
Flexible hours and leave arrangements help workers balance work with family life.
Regular feedback and recognition reward performance and reinforce commitment.

keyTerms.definition: Work done for a wage or salary under a contract with an employer.
Work done without financial reward, mainly in the home, such as child care and housework.
Unpaid work done by choice for people outside the household, usually through a charity or community group.
Paid work in which the worker earns income directly from their own trade, business or profession.
A document setting out a post's title, duties, working hours, pay range and required qualifications.
Satisfaction gained from rewards linked to work, such as pay, bonuses and job security, rather than from the task itself.
Satisfaction gained from the work itself, through fulfilment, creativity, challenge and pride.
The attitude a worker brings to work, shown through punctuality, commitment and respect for authority.
The level of achievement, advancement and recognition a person reaches through work.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between paid employment and unpaid work in the home, giving one feature of each.
questions.model: Paid employment is done for a wage or salary under a contract with an employer, and carries entitlements such as PRSI-based social insurance, pension and paid holidays. Unpaid work is done without financial reward, mainly in the home, such as child care, housework or caring for an elderly relative. Full marks need a feature for each type, not just a definition.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between extrinsic and intrinsic satisfaction at work. Discuss how each one can shape a worker's attitude to their job, giving an example occupation for each.
questions.model: Extrinsic satisfaction comes from rewards outside the task, such as pay, bonuses, job security and benefits. Intrinsic satisfaction comes from the work itself, such as challenge, creativity, responsibility and pride. Extrinsic rewards can keep a worker committed, especially in repetitive work such as assembly-line production, but they may bring less pride and self-esteem. Intrinsic satisfaction builds self-esteem, confidence and independence, and can give a worker status and a positive attitude to work, as in a professional or creative occupation. Strong intrinsic satisfaction often leads to a better work ethic and higher work attainment.
